concepts.name: Gupta Temple Architecture: Structural Evolution and Typology
key_dimensions: Transition from rock-cut to free-standing structural temples (flat-roofed to shikhara style)
Key examples: Dashavatara Temple (Deogarh), Bhitargaon Temple, Tigawa Temple — distinguishing features of each
Nagara style origins in Gupta period vs. later Dravidian developments — UPSC trap on which style is 'Gupta'
Use of Panchayatana plan layout and its first appearance in Gupta temples

concepts.name: Gupta Sculpture: Mathura vs. Sarnath Schools
key_dimensions: Mathura School: continuation from Kushana period, red sandstone, bold musculature, indigenous tradition
Sarnath School: fine white Chunar sandstone, transparent drapery ('wet drapery' effect), serene spiritual expression
UPSC trap: which school is 'purely Indian' vs. which retained Hellenistic influences
Comparison of Buddha image conventions: ushnisha, urna, mudras across both schools

concepts.name: Ajanta Caves: Gupta-Period Paintings and Their Iconographic Themes
key_dimensions: Identification of Gupta-period caves at Ajanta (Caves 16, 17, 19 — distinguishing from Satavahana-era caves 9, 10)
Tempera technique on wet plaster vs. true fresco — common UPSC misconception
Iconographic themes: Jataka tales, Mahajanaka Jataka, Padmapani Bodhisattva — significance
Naturalism, use of shading (modeling), and spatial depth as hallmarks of Gupta painting style

concepts.name: Bagh Caves Paintings: Distinction from Ajanta
key_dimensions: Location (Madhya Pradesh) and patronage context vs. Ajanta (Maharashtra)
Secular themes and more vibrant color palette compared to Ajanta's predominantly Buddhist themes
Similar tempera technique but different state of preservation — trap question on technique
Significance as evidence of Gupta painting tradition beyond a single site

concepts.name: Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh: Architectural and Iconographic Significance
key_dimensions: Earliest surviving example of a Panchayatana temple with a shikhara in Nagara style
Three surviving relief panels: Gajendramoksha, Nara-Narayana, Anantashayana Vishnu — iconographic details
UPSC trap: often called a 'Shaiva' temple but is actually Vaishnava
Architectural elements: garbhagriha, mandapa, decorative doorway (Shakha system)

concepts.name: Gupta Metal Sculpture: Copper and Bronze Casting Techniques
key_dimensions: Sultanganj Buddha (copper, Bihar) — largest known Gupta metal sculpture, cire-perdue (lost-wax) process
Bronze Buddha images from Mathura and Sarnath — stylistic continuity with stone sculpture
Iron Pillar of Delhi — not bronze but metallurgical achievement; UPSC often clubs it with Gupta art
Distinction between Gupta metal art and later Pala bronze tradition

concepts.name: Iron Pillar of Delhi: Metallurgical and Inscriptional Significance
key_dimensions: Attribution to Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) — Vishnudhvaja inscription in Sanskrit
Corrosion-resistant iron: phosphoric content and passive film theory — scientific significance
Original location debate: Mathura or Udayagiri, later moved to Delhi by Iltutmish — historical trap
Inscription content: military conquests, devotion to Vishnu — used as epigraphic source

concepts.name: Udayagiri Rock-Cut Caves: Political and Religious Iconography
key_dimensions: Location (Madhya Pradesh, near Vidisha) and direct Gupta imperial patronage (Chandragupta II)
Varaha panel: colossal Vishnu as Varaha rescuing Bhudevi — political symbolism of royal power
Cave 5 (Varaha) vs. Cave 6 (Shiva) — sectarian diversity within Gupta royal patronage
Inscription of Sanakanika chief — epigraphic evidence linking art and Gupta feudatory system

concepts.name: Gupta Coinage as Art: Iconographic and Dynastic Significance
key_dimensions: Gold coins (Dinars): types — Archer type, Lion-slayer type, Ashvamedha type — each associated with specific kings
Artistic quality: realistic portraiture and dynamic action scenes unlike earlier punch-marked coins
UPSC trap: Gupta coins as PRIMARY source for Gupta rulers' titles, epithets, and religious affiliations
Decline of Gupta coinage quality as indicator of empire's economic decline — numismatic evidence

concepts.name: Nagara Style of Temple Architecture: Origins and Gupta Contribution
key_dimensions: Defining features: curvilinear shikhara (latina type), amalaka, kalasha, absence of gopuram
Gupta period as the formative phase — Bhitargaon (terracotta shikhara) as transitional example
Sub-types of Nagara (Latina, Sekhari, Valabhi) — trap: only Latina type is associated with Gupta period
Comparison with Dravidian (pyramidal vimana, gopuram) and Vesara styles — UPSC frequently tests overlap

concepts.name: Terracotta Art in the Gupta Period: Continuity and Innovation
key_dimensions: Bhitargaon temple (UP): earliest surviving brick temple with terracotta decorative panels
Ahichchhatra and Rajghat terracotta figurines: yaksha, yakshi, and narrative plaques
Shift from moulded to hand-modelled terracotta — greater naturalism in Gupta period
UPSC trap: terracotta as a 'minor art' but significant for understanding popular/non-elite artistic tradition

concepts.name: Buddhist Art in the Gupta Period: Synthesis and Canonical Forms
key_dimensions: Standardization of Buddha iconography: 32 lakshanas, specific mudras (Dharmachakra, Abhaya, Dhyana) fixed in Gupta era
Gupta Buddha as the 'classical ideal' — influence on Southeast Asian Buddhist art (Java, Cambodia)
Nalanda as emerging Buddhist art center under Gupta patronage — continuity into Pala period
UPSC trap: Gandhara style (Hellenistic) vs. Gupta style (purely Indian) in representing the Buddha

concepts.name: Sanskrit Literature and Its Relationship with Gupta Artistic Patronage
key_dimensions: Kalidasa's descriptions in Meghaduta and Shakuntala as literary evidence for Gupta artistic aesthetic
Vishakhadatta's Mudrarakshasa and Devichandraguptam — dramatic arts as part of Gupta cultural milieu
Natyashastra (attributed to Bharata) — codification of performing arts parallel to visual art canonization
UPSC trap: distinguishing which texts are Gupta-period compositions vs. texts merely compiled/patronized during Gupta era

concepts.name: Ellora Caves: Gupta and Post-Gupta Transition in Rock-Cut Architecture
key_dimensions: Buddhist caves at Ellora (1–12): overlap of Gupta and Vakataka periods — not purely 'Gupta' (trap question)
Comparison with Ajanta: Ellora has more sculptural emphasis; Ajanta more known for paintings
Kailasa Temple (Cave 16) is Rashtrakuta, NOT Gupta — frequently confused in MCQs
Do-tala and Teen-tala monasteries at Ellora as evidence of Mahayana Buddhist art under Gupta influence

concepts.name: Vakataka–Gupta Artistic Synthesis: Political Alliance and Shared Aesthetic
key_dimensions: Marriage alliance: Chandragupta II's daughter Prabhavati Gupta married Rudrasena II (Vakataka) — political context
Ajanta caves patronized during Vakataka rule but stylistically follow Gupta aesthetic — attribution debate
Shared iconographic vocabulary across Gupta (Deogarh, Udayagiri) and Vakataka (Ajanta, Ramtek) sites
UPSC trap: crediting Ajanta entirely to 'Gupta Empire' when technically under Vakataka sovereignty

concepts.name: Gupta Art: Concept of 'Classical Age' — Characteristics and Historiographical Debate
key_dimensions: Defining features of Gupta 'classicism': balance, harmony, spiritual serenity, idealization of human form
Criticism of 'Golden Age' label: exclusion of women, lower castes; Vincent Smith vs. Romila Thapar perspectives
Continuity from earlier periods (Kushana, Satavahana) vs. Gupta innovation — UPSC tests whether Gupta art is revolutionary or evolutionary
Influence on subsequent art traditions: Pallava, Pala, and Southeast Asian — as measure of 'classical' status

concepts.name: Gupta Manuscript Illumination and Minor Arts: Ivory, Textiles, and Gems
key_dimensions: Earliest surviving illuminated Buddhist manuscripts attributed to Gupta/post-Gupta period (palm-leaf manuscripts)
Fa-Hien's account as primary source for craft traditions, ivory work, and textile trade in Gupta India
Arthashastra and Amarakosha references to craft guilds (shreni) — institutional support for minor arts
UPSC trap: distinguishing between Gupta-period minor arts evidence (textual) vs. surviving material evidence (limited)

concepts.name: Mathura as an Artistic Center: Pre-Gupta to Gupta Continuity
key_dimensions: Mathura School's roots in Kushana period — Kanishka headless statue, early Buddha images
Gupta transformation: from Kushana boldness to Gupta spiritual refinement in the SAME center
Mathura's role as a crossroads: Jain, Buddhist, and Brahmanical art all produced simultaneously — sectarian pluralism
UPSC trap: assuming Mathura School is exclusively Buddhist; significant Jain tirthankara images also from Mathura
